Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say.
A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference.
Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition.

articles.title_zh: China cuts US Treasury holdings to 18-year low in August as debt fears mount
articles.content_orig:
Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Business news – live updates
Larry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is coming
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.
US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.
The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September , marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.
The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
after newsletter promotion
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
articles.content_orig:
Trump: New White House press secretary should 'reconsider' job
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.
US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
Hours later, praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him.
As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.
Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president.
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
"When I was in China," she replied.
After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"
Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In the president's first term, Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

The greatest compliment you could pay the All Blacks for dissecting Australia was that their dominance and ruthlessness were Springbok-esque, comprehensively popping the Wallabies’ recent bubble under head coach Les Kiss.
Both teams came into this contest at the All Blacks’ Eden Park fortress having last played South Africa: Australia knocked off the world champions in Perth while New Zealand lost the Greatest Rivalry series 3-1 .
A telling feature of those matches was the Springboks’ aerial dominance, which Australia would have studied hard given the spring-heeled backs at their disposal.
Yet the All Blacks immediately put that hard-earned lesson into practice in Auckland where Cam Roigard, the scrum-half, put up a succession of high balls that the New Zealand backs, led by the excellent Jordie Barrett, retrieved almost at will. At one stage, Beauden Barrett pinched the ball directly from the grasp of Joseph-Aukuso Sua’ali’i, who was not so long ago considered the best high-ball player in the world.
The All Blacks’ supremacy in this department soon spread elsewhere turning a close-fought first-half contest – 17-14 – into a blowout.
Kiss would have been delighted by his side’s ball movement in the first half, which yielded tries for Tom Wright and Harry Wilson as they looked to extend the head coach’s unbeaten record. That came to a shuddering halt in the second half when the All Blacks started dominating the breakdown and contact area.
The wave of forward carries, which resulted in their fourth try scored by hooker Codie Taylor, again bore a certain resemblance to the Boks’ pack power. So too New Zealand’s refusal to let their foot off Australia’s throat in a second half, which they won 33-5.
It means the Bledisloe Cup will remain in New Zealand’s possession for an astonishing 24th successive year, while their winning run against the Wallabies now extends to 12 successive games. It was all the more impressive that this was achieved without back-row talisman and fly-half Ruben Love, one of New Zealand’s leading lights in the Greatest Rivalry series.
That mantle was taken on by half-backs Roigard and Damian McKenzie, who delivered one of his best performances in the All Blacks No 10 shirt. It was his incisive broken-field runs that provided the momentum for flankers Peter Lakai and Tupou Vaa’i to score tries. Yet at this stage, the All Blacks were in a game with referee Andrew Brace pinging them for offside while Jeremy Williams was causing them just as many problems at the lineout.
The Wallabies’ handling was also sharp with some delightful interplay between Ben Donaldson and Max Jorgensen allowing Wright to go over for the first try. Their second was equally well-worked, with Donaldson sweeping behind a pod of forwards before feeding captain Wilson. McKenzie’s penalty proved the only difference between the sides at the break.
How Australia will rue their start to the second half when they kicked a penalty to within five metres of the All Blacks tryline only to concede a penalty for obstruction at the maul. A three-point deficit would soon become 30.
Roigard was central to everything and is laying a strong claim to displacing Antoine Dupont as the world’s greatest scrum-half. His box kicks appeared laser-guided and even when Donaldson claimed one, he was enveloped in a black tide, conceding a penalty. With that foothold, an All Blacks maul came up just short, but Roigard sniped past an unguarded ruck.
After the forwards provided the platform for Taylor’s try, Roigard brilliantly changed the direction of the attack twice in one move which resulted in Leroy Carter’s score, although the winger was injured in the process. No matter, as his replacement Josh Moorby got the All Blacks’ sixth. While Josh Nasser scored a consolation try for Australia, Will Jordan’s converted score brought up New Zealand’s half-century.

articles.title_orig: Benjamin Satterley, wrestler known as Pac, died of bronchial asthma
articles.title_zh: Benjamin Satterley, wrestler known as Pac, died of bronchial asthma
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Satterley, known to wrestling fans around the world as Pac, died last month of bronchial asthma , the medical examiner’s office in Cook County, Illinois, confirmed Friday.
The manner of death was natural, the office said.
Satterley, 40, died Sept. 27, just one day after having wrestled on All Elite Wrestling’s “All Out” pay-per-view. His death sent waves of shock and grief across the world of professional wrestling.
The New York Post first reported the cause of death.
He was found in Des Plaines, around 2 miles north of the Chicago O’Hare International Airport, the medical examiner’s office said at the time.
Satterley came up through the British independent system before making the leap to Japan and the U.S. A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, he became a highly influential figure known both for his hard-hitting style and breathtaking aerial abilities.
He went on to earn global acclaim, wrestling for some of the top promotions in the world, including AEW, World Wrestling Entertainment (where he went by Adrian Neville), New Japan Pro-Wrestling and Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre.
Satterley adopted the moniker of “The Bastard” at AEW, and captivated fans and contemporaries with the speed, grace, precision and power through which he moved in the ring. On the microphone, his promos conveyed a no-nonsense intensity that equally gripped viewers.
At a time when the fourth wall between fan and wrestler had long collapsed, Satterley rarely broke character. Yet, his death highlighted the humility and kindness behind “The Bastard” persona.
“He was just so modest about how fascinating he was,” Marina Shafir, a fellow member of the Death Riders stable of which Satterley was a part, said at an indie show hours after his death.
“I wouldn’t be here today if I didn’t share time and space with this man,” she said.
Days after his death, AEW turned its weekly “Dynamite” show into an emotional tribute to its fallen star, nicknamed “The Man That Gravity Forgot.”
“Whilst he will always have a legacy as one of the greatest wrestlers the U.K. has ever produced, we have been so glad to see so many wonderful tributes that acknowledged who Ben was as a person,” the Satterley family said in a statement read during the show. “He exemplified what it meant to be a decent human being, an honorable man with principles, who adored his family and his sausage dog son, Wolfie.”
On Instagram, his wife, Natalie, thanked Satterley “for our beautiful life.”
“We will try our hardest to get through this nightmare and look after each other as I know that’s what you would want,” she wrote, “but we will miss you every minute, of every hour, of every day.”
Rudy Chinchilla is a breaking news editor for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
articles.title_zh: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
articles.content_orig:
Israeli settlers brutally attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a photojournalist working for The Washington Post in the occupied West Bank on Friday, beating villagers and setting olive groves ablaze.
The attack was among several targeting Palestinians trying to gather their olive harvest, with further assaults and arson reported in nearby communities as well.
These incidents are just the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms on local communities in the West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.
Veteran journalist Heidi Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault on Friday in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. A Palestinian man was also shot in the thigh by Israeli soldiers, according to a witness who spoke to Al Jazeera and the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.
Levine, an American freelance photojournalist who works for The Washington Post, fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.
Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported.
Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said.
As they helped her towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. Levine was eventually taken to hospital in Ramallah.
Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said.
“They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the man was eventually taken away in an ambulance.
Wafa also reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added.
Matt Murray, executive editor of The Washington Post, said in a statement: “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”
Several US lawmakers expressed outrage.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen wrote n a post on X, that the “repeated violence and brazen impunity for attacks” against Americans and Palestinians alike are “unacceptable”. “When will Trump and Rubio DO SOMETHING?”
He urged the administration to hold those responsible to account.
In posts on X, US Congressman Ro Khanna highlighted the assault on Levine, saying that attackers “picked her up, then threw her down again and kept kicking”.
Khanna called for an end to US assistance, saying: “We need to cut off aid to Israel that is used to fund settler activity, and stop the sales of these weapons.”
Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro also called for accountability. “If the settlers will do this to an American journalist on camera, in broad daylight, imagine what Palestinian families face when no one is watching,” she wrote in a post on X.
“Those responsible for this attack must be held accountable.”
There was violence in other parts of the occupied West Bank on Friday, as well. In Burqa, east of Ramallah, four Palestinians were reported to have been injured in a settler attack on olive pickers. In nearby Turmus Aya, settlers assaulted farmers and burned vehicles and olive trees. A civil defence volunteer was also injured, according to Wafa.
The attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians gathering olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.
Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted. On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.
The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks, and have stepped up as the seasonal Palestinian olive harvest gets under way.
The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has recorded at least 170 pogroms since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, Reuters reported.
The violence threatens Palestinian livelihoods and access to their land. Farmers endure assaults, the destruction of trees and the theft of crops, while settlers have also begun stealing olives from Palestinian-owned groves themselves.
Al Jazeera correspondent Tareq Abu Azzoum reported that the intimidation extends beyond agricultural land to Palestinian homes and vehicles, creating pressure on communities to leave.
“People there are still living under threat of attack, not just on their agricultural lands, but also on their properties,” he said.
“Vehicles and houses have been repeatedly hit by settler attacks, which have been used by the Israeli military, apparently, to create a deterrent environment with Palestinians expected to leave these areas so they can later turn them into Israeli settlements.”

articles.title_zh: With flying Roadster, Tesla waves goodbye to the car business
articles.content_orig:
Tesla unveiled its long-anticipated Roadster on Thursday during a dramatic event in which the vehicle used compressed-air thrusters to fly off a ramp and perform a midair maneuver.
Tesla unveiled its long-anticipated Roadster on Thursday during a dramatic event in which the vehicle used compressed-air thrusters to fly off a ramp and perform a midair maneuver.
The vehicle was seen flying, performing a midair flip and accelerating from zero to 60 mph in under a second.
"Turns out the future does have flying cars," Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas.
Vice President of Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy added, "Flying cars are real."
ELON MUSK CALLS WAYMO CARS 'PET DESTROYERS' AS ROBOTAXI RIVALS CLASH OVER SAFETY
Tesla officially unveiled its redesigned, next-generation Roadster on Oct. 15, 2026, during a dramatic livestreamed event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas. (Tesla/X)
The jaw-dropping showcase featured the new Roadster accelerating up a massive curved ramp and using a fan-based suction system to remain attached until it was completely upside down before using integrated cold-gas thrusters developed in collaboration with SpaceX to launch off the ramp, flip in midair and land safely back on the ground.
In another demonstration, the Roadster launched over a lineup of cars and a semi-truck, performing a midair flip before landing safely on the other side.
Musk said certain versions of the Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than one second and reach a top speed of more than 230 mph. During the event, Tesla demonstrated a Roadster accelerating to 60 mph in under a second.
WATCH: ROADSTER PERFORMS ‘KICK FLIP’ STUNT:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk introduced a flight demonstration Thursday in Texas of a next-generation Tesla Roadster electric vehicle performing a "kick flip" over other Tesla vehicles.
"Every car on the road today is limited by one thing: tire grip Roadster's thruster system generates 4–5x the force the tires can. More force on the same mass means significantly better acceleration – physics does the rest," Tesla said on X.
Nearly a decade after the Roadster's initial 2017 concept debut, the vehicle left audiences in awe with the gravity-defying demonstration that deployed SpaceX’s rocket technology.
"Today, Roadster presents a new moment in history – the best of the last human-driven cars," Tesla wrote on X.
Tesla executives announced at Thursday's event that production would begin in 2028.
Tesla's next-generation Roadster launched over a lineup of cars and a semi-truck, performing a midair flip before landing safely on the other side. (Tesla/X)
Musk and other Tesla executives did not outline the cost at Thursday's event, but nearly a decade ago, the company quoted a base price of $200,000.

articles.title_orig: China: Japan needs to face history and reflect on past crimes
articles.title_zh: China: Japan needs to face history and reflect on past crimes
articles.content_orig:
Japan can only truly move toward the future by thoroughly reflecting on its wartime aggression and sincerely repenting for its crimes, the Chinese defense ministry said on Friday.
Senior Colonel Chen Xi, spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks when commenting on renewed public attention to the atrocities committed by Unit 731 of the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.
His comments came after documentaries in Singapore and Japan drew renewed attention to Unit 731. A Singapore-produced documentary, Inside Unit 731: Japan's Secret Human Experiments, was recently named the best history documentary and has drawn more than 1.45 million views on YouTube.
Japan's public broadcaster NHK also aired a documentary titled The Secret Unit: The Silent Postwar Era, which used newly discovered photographs and testimony from people with firsthand knowledge to examine crimes committed by Unit 731.
Chen said Unit 731 carried out inhumane experiments on living people and conducted biological warfare during Japan's invasion of China, acts that seriously violated international law and constituted grave crimes against humanity.
"The historical truth will not disappear, and the evidence of the crimes committed by the invading Japanese forces is irrefutable and cannot be denied," Chen said, citing views expressed by people in Japan who have called for an honest reckoning with the country's wartime history.
He also said recent attempts by Japanese right-wing forces to use emerging technologies to tamper with data and distort public understanding of history had again raised concerns in the international community.
Chen said efforts to whitewash Japan's wartime aggression or deny historical facts would not change the record of what happened.

articles.title_orig: Trump pauses new Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump pauses new Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
President signed the legislation championed by late senator Lindsey Graham last month but has waived the restrictions as they were due to come into effect
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
In an executive order on Friday, the US president said he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a ​new leader.
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The legislation – whose ‌ primary backer in ‌Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The president has face widespread criticism after making the announcement, with a dozen US senators – including six Republicans – calling on Trump ⁠to rescind his diesel deal.
A letter from the bipartisan group of lawmakers sent on Tuesday urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the legislation passed last month, called the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026”.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until 18 October to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Zelenskyy said on Friday the diesel deal would mean cash “will start flowing back into Russia”, as he met European leaders in Brussels .
Trump ⁠blindsided Zelenskyy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. Facing midterm elections next month, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for ​pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US ‌Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph (161km/h). Neither has officially been confirmed.
The US sanctions legislation has also become a campaign centerpiece for Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister appointed to serve out the remaining months of his term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
In a debate earlier this week with South Carolina Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was Trump’s purview as to how he implemented it.
“It gives the president tools that he can use, if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said during the debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”
With Reuters and the Associated Press

articles.title_orig: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.title_zh: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.content_orig:
The Bryson Fire burns in Malibu, Calif., on Oct. 15, 2026. The brush fire in the mountains west of Los Angeles prompted evacuation warnings from officials, as powerful Santa Ana winds risked spreading the blaze rapidly.
Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season have arrived, igniting multiple blazes across the region.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening followed a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California . Only 300,000 acres had burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong , according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
The largest fire, named the Henderson fire, erupted Thursday afternoon around Camp Pendleton, a San Diego Marine Corps training base, and had burned through 1,404 acres by Friday morning. Two other fires have burned through 200 acres and 43 acres in Los Angeles county.
The NWS issued a red flag warning on Oct. 15 for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
As of Thursday night, Southern California Edison shut off power to tens of thousands of customers. Nearly 90,000 PG&E customers were also left without power. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or discarded cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

articles.title_orig: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
articles.title_zh: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
articles.content_orig:
Justice department warns election officials of prosecution if they ‘knowingly tabulate ballots’ cast by noncitizens
The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month’s midterm elections , warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
The letter on Friday from senior justice department officials and obtained first by the Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort to investigate noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections has only turned up a handful of cases so far. The justice department has charged about 50 people who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens out of the more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
“The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime – and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the justice department.
It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”
The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles county counsel’s office and also is copied to the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, and the Los Angeles county registrar, Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.
Trump weighed in late Friday, sharing on Truth Social a link to a news story about the letter and adding: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”
The justice department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the 3 November election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution”.
“It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election,” he said.
Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general who teaches at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, dismissed the idea that an attempted prosecution of an election official using the letter’s rationale would hold up.
“Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course,” he said. “Fortunately, election officials – not just in Los Angeles, but across the country – are equipped to stand up to aggressive bullying. And the law is on their side.”
More than 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the US House for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidential term.
Earlier Friday, Alex Padilla, California Democratic senator, Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democratic senator and Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democratic senator, wrote to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, demanding that the justice department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
ROCHESTER, Minn. — The older sister of embattled Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., who is currently on a book tour promoting a memoir about her life as a Somali immigrant, skipped a scheduled event due to a "family emergency" amid the fallout from the raid on the congresswoman's home.
As Omar faces a federal government probe related to potential immigration fraud as well as a separate investigation into her financial disclosures, Sahra Noor was scheduled for a book tour stop at the University of Minnesota Rochester on Thursday night.
Noor, who came to the United States as a refugee alongside Omar and other family members in the 1990s, was reportedly subpoenaed in relation to the immigration investigation into her sister. She currently lives in Nairobi, Kenya, according to her LinkedIn page, but is on a worldwide book tour promoting her recently-released "Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story."
Ilhan Omar wearing a patterned hijab and green scarf. (L) Sahra Noor, sister of Ilhan Omar, speaking at an event at the University of Minnesota in 2016. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images; University of Minnesota)
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION
Fox News Digital reached out to Noor for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.
According to a flyer, which was posted on Facebook by Rochester-based bookstore Garden Party Books, the event was scheduled for Thursday night at 6:30 p.m. It was set to be held at the Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota Rochester.
When Fox News Digital arrived for the event, the space was completely empty. Fox News Digital had previously RSVP'd for the event via a QR code on the flyer and did not receive any communication that the event had been canceled, rescheduled or relocated.
Garden Party Books told Fox News Digital the event was canceled due to a Noor "family emergency."
The Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota, Rochester, Minnesota, Thursday, October 14, 2026. Sahra Noor, sister of Rep. Ilhan  Omar, was scheduled to discuss her memoir, Salt in the Snow at this location but for an undisclosed reason the event was canceled without warning. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)
Noor's absence from the book tour stop comes amid rumors that Omar fled the United States following the raid earlier this week. While the congresswoman has not been seen in public since Monday's raid, her husband snapped when asked outside the home on Wednesday whether he had a response to the rumors that she fled the country.
The flyer said that Garden Party Books, along with the University of Minnesota Bookstores and the Rochester Public Library, were "proud supporters" of the event.
It also described Noor as a "poet, storyteller and health system leader," and said the book is a "story of migration, motherhood, grief and family."
According to Noor's website , her book was officially launched during an event in a Nairobi bookstore on Aug. 13, 2026. She appeared in early September at a festival in Cape Town, South Africa to promote her work.
OMAR RAID DRAWS OMINOUS WARNING FROM VANCE AS HE BLASTS PROGRESSIVE REP'S 'RAGE' TOWARD AMERICA
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
Now, she is touring in the United States. Noor held an Oct. 1 event in Minneapolis, and another five days later at the University of Minnesota. She hosted an event in St. Paul, Minnesota on Oct. 7. Her next scheduled event is at the Somali Community Cultural Innovation Hub in Seattle on Oct. 23.
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the leading investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Omar's home starting at around 6:00 a.m. on Monday morning.
ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID
Fox News Digital first reported Monday that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago.
The investigation, two sources noted, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid.
Omar has described the search as an "outrageous abuse of power" and called it an "unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

articles.title_orig: Norte Fire burning near San Juan Capistrano prompts evacuation orders as flames threaten homes
articles.title_zh: Norte Fire burning near San Juan Capistrano prompts evacuation orders as flames threaten homes
articles.content_orig:
Crews are battling a wildfire, dubbed the Norte Fire, that is threatening homes in the San Juan Capistrano area on Friday afternoon.
The Orange County Fire Authority said firefighters responded to the area of Portico Del Norte shortly after 11:30 a.m. after receiving reports of the fire.
"In anticipation of the fire weather that we're currently experiencing, we had upstaffed a bunch of resources and placed them in strategic areas to anticipate potential fires and their growth," OCFA Battalion Chief Mark Backhoff said.
Firefighters said the topography, coupled with the weather, allowed the fire to quickly grow to 570 acres and prompted evacuation orders.
The OCFA said crews are aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air.  Aerial footage showed helicopters and planes dropping water and fire retardant as flames burned several homes. The OCFA said the fire impacted six homes.
Two firefighters were hospitalized with significant injuries but are in stable condition, according to the OCFA.
"I've lived here since 1995, and this is the first time we've really ever had a fire in this area," resident Robert Morris said. "It's a wake-up call."
Crews knocked down the majority of the fire by 5:45 p.m., according to Capt. Steve Concialdi.
"We still have some homes that are impacted here," he said. "As you can see, the wind is still blowing pretty strong up here."
State officials secured a FEMA grant to provide additional resources to crews in Orange County.
"By securing this federal assistance, we are ensuring our local and state partners have the critical resources they need to aggressively fight the Norte Fire, protect lives and property, and keep Californians safe," Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote in a statement.
Agencies from LA County and San Bernardino County sent resources to help OCFA throughout the fire.
"Our community will get through this together," San Juan Capistrano Mayor John Campbell said. "Right now, our focus is on protecting life, supporting those who have been displaced, and giving our first responders the space and resources they need to continue their work."
Evacuation orders have been issued for San Juan Zones 4, 5 and 10. They have also been issued for San Clemente Zones 12 and 13.
"Follow the evacuation orders because we never know when the wind will change," County Supervisor Katrina Foley said. "That's what we saw during the Airport Fire. We don't want anyone to get hurt."
"Please be patient with us right now. We know you want to get back into your homes," Concialdi said. "We have a lot of firefighters working ... We don't want to see any more homes be damaged from this fire."
A Santa Ana wind event and hot temperatures have elevated fire danger across Southern California. A heat advisory will be in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday for inland Orange County and coastal areas across Southern California. Temperatures are expected to reach up to 95 degrees, increasing the risk of heat-related illness.
Concialdi said crews are attempting to put out embers and hotspots to prevent the Santa Ana winds from spreading the fire.
"When we have Santa Ana winds, they could blow embers a mile, even greater," Concialdi said.
He added that OCFA's firefighting helicopters will continue to fly amid the windy conditions.
"If there's a threat, they'll be flying," Concialdi said.
The South Coast Air Quality Management District said the smoke and particles from the Norte Fire will degrade air quality to levels unhealthy for sensitive groups by Friday evening in parts of South Orange County, including San Clemente, Dana Point, San Juan Capistrano and Laguna Niguel. It is expected to remain at that level until Saturday morning.
AQMD said the air quality will be good to moderate for most of South Orange County by Saturday afternoon. It urged residents to remain indoors with windows and doors closed, use their air conditioners and air purifiers, but avoid swamp coolers or fans that can bring in outside air.
It also recommended residents use N95 or P100 respirators if they must go outside.
"Remain vigilant and listen to emergency officials as we continue to face high Santa Ana winds and work to suppress the Norte Fire in Orange County," Newsom wrote on a post to X.
San Diego Gas and Electric, which operates the power utilities in the area, said an outage that started at 11:31 a.m. affected about 496 customers during the fire.
Another outage that affected 2,351 customers near the fire appeared later in the afternoon.
As a precaution, Santa Margarita Water District asked residents in the area to conserve water.
"Our firefighters have had no issues getting water onto this fire," OCFA Chief TJ McGovern said. "I know that the Santa Margarita Water District is asking all residents to follow their standard wildfire protocol ... Again, we have no issues, and this is a precautionary measure."
The California Highway Patrol closed the Ortega Highway onramp to the southbound 5 Freeway. Authorities asked people to avoid the area.
The northbound 5 Freeway through San Diego County was closed earlier in the day for another fire, but it was reopened by 5:30 p.m.
"We just need people to stay off the I-5, stay off the freeway because it's impacted," Foley said.

articles.title_orig: Iran Is Giving Houthis Targeting and Intelligence for Attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Iran Is Giving Houthis Targeting and Intelligence for Attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.
Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London who took part in Yemen’s 2011 uprising and later negotiated with the Houthis, told Iran International’s Eye for Iran podcast that Tehran’s involvement began long before the group became a major regional force.
His account comes as Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure have opened another front in the wider war, threatening aviation and trade routes already disrupted by the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz.
“I think we’re entering phase three,” Shiban said, describing what he sees as Tehran’s strategy of extending the economic cost of the war to US allies.
Iran, he argued, had kept the Houthis in reserve as a strategic asset until it needed them. Their attacks now serve Tehran’s interests while advancing the group’s own ambitions inside Yemen.
From democracy conferences to an IRGC handler
Young Yemenis who took part in the 2011 Arab Spring were invited to conferences in Lebanon that were presented as discussions of democratic reform, Shiban said. Those who went found that Hezbollah operatives were behind them.
Activists receptive to Iran’s revolutionary ideology were introduced to a Revolutionary Guards officer working in Lebanon under the alias Abu Hadi, he said, and some went on to Tehran.
“We were calling it the Arab Spring. The Iranians called it the Islamic Awakening,” he said. Tehran, he said, wanted to present Yemen’s uprising as an extension of Iran’s 1979 revolution.
Shiban identified the officer as Hassan Irlou , who in 2020 became Iran’s ambassador to the Houthi authorities in Sanaa, a post the United States said was held by a Quds Force official. Irlou died in December 2021.
Hezbollah ran much of the operation at first, Shiban said, before Revolutionary Guards personnel took a more prominent role.
The recruitment reached beyond political activists to women invited to conferences in Iran, some of whom came back converted to the Islamic Republic’s ideology. Shiban said he was shocked by one woman he knew as very liberal, who had protested alongside him and returned from Iran repeating Tehran’s case for crushing the Syrian revolution.
“She has absorbed that propaganda of what the Iranians were saying about the Syrian revolution and why they need to kill all of those protesters until the last one, given this woman herself was protesting with us,” he said.
People drawn into these networks went on to help set up the Houthis’ political bureau in Sanaa, Shiban said. Iran International could not independently verify the full extent of the recruitment he described.
The account has new weight after Saudi Arabia disclosed on Thursday that the Houthis had rejected an invitation to negotiations in Oman in July.
Riyadh had sought talks to settle outstanding differences before the fighting escalated, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly said.
The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh 20 times in October. At least 19 people have been killed in the recent attacks across the kingdom, according to Saudi officials.
Yemen analyst Fatima Alasrar said on X that the Houthis’ refusal reflected Tehran’s timetable rather than an effort to resolve their long-standing demands over airport access, and warned that Iran could keep leverage through the Bab el-Mandeb strait even if it reached a deal with Washington over Hormuz.
The Houthis also have their own aims, among them consolidating control over Yemen and forcing Saudi Arabia to end its support for rival Yemeni forces.
A second strategic chokepoint
The war has put Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, at the center of the regional confrontation.
Iran saw the leverage that disrupting Hormuz gave it and wanted the same at a second shipping route, Shiban said. “It saw how valuable and important the Strait of Hormuz was and it wanted to add another choke point.”
The consequences are visible inside Yemen. On Thursday, Houthi missiles struck the presidential palace compound in Aden, killing five people, according to Yemeni authorities. Houthi advances around Taiz have intensified fighting and displacement.
The escalation could prove costly for Tehran, Shiban said, having already antagonized Saudi Arabia and pushed Yemen’s internationally recognized government toward wider war. But Iran’s leaders appear willing to take that risk, he said, on the calculation that Western governments will hesitate to act decisively.
“I think right now they’re counting on the United States is going to be hesitant,” he said.
Even a long confrontation could suit Tehran, he said, if it raises the economic pressure on the Persian Gulf states and strains their ties with Washington.
You can watch Eye for Iran on YouTube or listen on any podcast platform.
Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.
Ayoub Mohammad Nabil, from Haditha in western Iraq, was hanged on Sunday morning at Lakan Prison in Rasht, the capital of Gilan province on the Caspian coast, the group said. Iranian officials and domestic media had not reported his sentence or his execution by the time it was announced.
Nabil had entered Iran legally on his passport and was working as a caretaker at a private villa when Intelligence Ministry agents arrested him in the nearby town of Fouman on August 26, 2025. He had no prior security record, Iran Human Rights said.
A source told the group he was held for about five months at the Intelligence Ministry’s detention center in Rasht, where he was subjected to severe psychological torture. He denied any link to Saudi Arabia or groups tied to it, and said he had been accused because he was a practicing Sunni Muslim, wore a beard and taught the Quran to local children in his guardhouse.
Despite no evidence of any political activity, the source said, Branch One of Rasht’s Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death for “moharebeh,” or waging war against God, through spying for Saudi-backed proxy groups.
The Kurdish rights group Hengaw, citing its own sources, said Nabil was moved to solitary confinement for execution on October 8, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis intensified.
He is at least the 17th person executed in Iran on espionage charges this year, and the third Iraqi, according to Iran Human Rights. Thirteen were accused of spying for Israel or the United States; the other two Iraqis were accused of spying for an unnamed Arab country, and an Afghan man for an unnamed state. Fifteen of the 17 were executed after the war began in February.
More than 70 political prisoners have been executed in Iran since the January protests, and at least 20 more face execution on political charges, Iran International has found.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a report on Thursday that capital cases in Iran, especially security cases, involve systematic violations of fair-trial rights, including forced confessions, closed trials lasting minutes and restricted access to independent lawyers. He called for an immediate halt to executions.
The rights group HRANA said last week that at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran in the year to October 8, up 29 percent on the previous year.

articles.title_orig: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
articles.title_zh: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
articles.content_orig:
When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.
There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.
Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.
At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.
In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.
However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.
In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.
Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.
And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.
But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.
Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are  Chinese EVs.
It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.
This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.
The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.
Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".
It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.
But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

articles.title_orig: Trump Waives Many Russia-Related Sanctions, Tariffs In Relief For India, China
articles.title_zh: Trump Waives Many Russia-Related Sanctions, Tariffs In Relief For India, China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump prevented some new sanctions on Russia and hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian oil from taking effect late Friday, waiving portions of a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring the Russian government — as Mr. Trump seeks to ease prices by tapping Russian energy.
Tariffs of 100% on the world's five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas were set to take effect on Sunday under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which Mr. Trump signed late last month . But the law gives the president the authority to waive portions of the law if he certifies to Congress that halting the sanctions is "in the national interests of the United States," a provision that Mr. Trump invoked in an executive order Friday.
The president said he sent a notification to Congress.
He also waived the law's 500% tariffs on Russian goods, and halted certain other sanctions on Russia. He said the waivers will remain in place until administration officials "determine that further action is appropriate," and directed members of his administration to "monitor" countries that import Russian energy or evade sanctions.
The law — championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died before it was passed — largely took aim at the world's largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China, India and Turkey. The European Union has also historically purchased large quantities of natural gas from Russia, but it has cut imports significantly in recent years.
The Friday night waivers came one week after Mr. Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.
The moves mark an about-face for the United States, which has imposed tight restrictions on Russian oil and gas for years — and urged other countries to follow suit — in an effort to prevent Putin from using his country's energy wealth to finance his invasion of Ukraine.
But as oil prices remain high after spiking due to the Iran war, Mr. Trump has increasingly turned his attention to Russia and Ukraine, arguing that war has pushed up energy prices.
Mr. Trump pressed both countries to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure last weekend, announcing an "energy ceasefire." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially said he was willing to abide by an energy ceasefire, but after Russian attacks continued, he said earlier this week that Ukraine would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries.
The U.S. president has lashed out at Zelenskyy, saying he is "not a big fan."
The decision to ease sanctions has drawn pushback in Congress. Earlier this week, a bipartisan group of senators called the diesel waivers a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine," and urged Mr. Trump to enforce the sanctions and tariffs laid out in the Graham law.
"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," they wrote.

articles.title_orig: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.title_zh: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.content_orig:
Two of the victims were five-year-old Rhoam Summer (left) and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25 (right)
Some readers may find this article distressing.
An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen.
The bystander, a father of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend on Thursday lunchtime when he saw the suspect firing in the car park, then shooting through a window to enter.
Police said the 16-year-old suspect used to be a student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Watch: Mother of Oregon school shooting 'hero' recounts call with son
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station her son had called her moments after the shooting, and he was "traumatised".
"He said a man went into my daughter's school," Freeman said, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mom."
She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, mom, I couldn't save them all."
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China Could Fully Stop Production Of Cars With Hidden Door Handles
articles.title_zh: China Could Fully Stop Production Of Cars With Hidden Door Handles
articles.content_orig:
China's market regulator has drafted rules that would sharply limit fully electric hidden door handles starting January 1, 2027. Doors would still need to open if the power fails.
The draft also sets a July 1, 2027 paperwork deadline for models already on sale and spells out when a hidden-handle design could trigger a production halt.
The retractable door handles of the Tesla Model S
From January 1, 2027, any manufacturer applying to register a new vehicle design in China would have to submit extra technical data and safety-validation material if that design uses what regulators call an "innovative" feature, with hidden door handles high on the list. The rule targets fully flush, power-retracting handles that sit level with the body and pop out electronically.
Under the draft, fully electric external handles that depend on power to present and release would be banned. Semi-hidden or recessed designs could stay, but only if the handle can be operated mechanically and offers a grab space of at least 2.4 inches by 0.8 inch for a hand to pull.
The draft does not stop at door handles. The same rules would require physical controls for safety-critical functions like exterior lights, windshield wipers, and defogging, shifting those tasks away from touchscreen-only menus.
Vehicles already approved for sale in China are not exempt from the new rules. Automakers have until July 1, 2027 to submit extra technical and validation materials for any already certified model, including the China-market BMW iX3 without pop-out handles . A separate door-handle safety standard gives those in-market vehicles a longer transition period to complete any hardware changes.
Recessed Door Handle Design
Compliance is not just about adding a lever. Reports on the draft describe 51 additional parameters regulators want documented for new vehicle registrations, covering structural and software reliability, environmental adaptability, heating and cooling performance, and sealing against water and dust.
Innovative designs also face real-world durability testing with at least 18,600 miles.
That does not mean every car with flush handles gets pulled from the road. The production-halt and recall rules only apply to vehicles that miss the documentation deadline and are later found to carry a genuine safety risk.
The risk sits with automakers that let the July 2027 deadline lapse on a model with an undocumented or weakly tested design. In that case, the draft calls for an immediate production stop and a recall plan filed with the regulator, similar to the Tesla door handle recall in China .

articles.title_orig: Chi and Uznik lead shock in Salt Lake City
articles.title_zh: Chi and Uznik lead shock in Salt Lake City
articles.content_orig:
Men’s qualification signalled the start of the final World Climbing Series event for Boulder, and it threw up one of the surprises of the 2026 season
Out of the 78 men that started the competition in Salt Lake City, USA, and the 24 that made in through into the semi-final, there was one name that stuck out – and not because he made it, but because surprisingly he didn’t.
Japan’s Sorato Anraku was on for an unprecedented six wins from six World Climbing Series events in the same season for the men, but that dream came to an end as he finished in 29 th overall in the qualification round.
That exit from the competition means that there will be a new name on the 2026 Boulder gold medal list, and USA’s Auggie Chi and Austria’s Nicolai Uznik are the early frontrunners sharing the top spot.
Split into two, Chi and Uznik led their respective groups for a share of the Salt Lake City lead going into the semi-final stage. Chi had 109.9pts and Uznik had 95pts.
Max Bertone was the early leader with 109.3pts, but Chi came out to drop the Frenchman down a place into third alongside Japan’s next hope, Rei Kawamata who had 94.9pts.
From this point down the scores started to bunch up in both groups with fifth placed Mejdi Schalck of France and Great Britain’s Max Milne posting similar scores despite being in different groups – Schalck had 94.9pts, Milne 94.8pts.
In seventh there were four climbers with both groups unable to split their athletes. USA’s Colin Duffy and Great Britain’s Toby Roberts scored 94.7pts in their group and Italy’s Luca Boldrini and Japan’s Sohta Amagasa scored 94.6pts in theirs.
Speaking after his round home nation climber Duffy said: “It was a good round. I enjoyed the boulders and the atmosphere here at a home event for me a lot. Two of the boulders in the round were super hard so you had to be very efficient in the rest of the round, which I think I accomplished.”
Reflecting on his season Duffy said: “I think it's been my best season in Boulder since I've been on the circuit and it's very exciting to finish it here in the US.”
The Salt Lake City event has been on the calendar for a few seasons now, but the venue has moved this year to the city’s baseball stadium, and Duffy is a fan of the move: “I think this is a step up from where we've had previous events here in Salt Lake City. Bringing climbing to a bigger stadium with this atmosphere is the future. I hope the fans are sitting comfortably and enjoying the climbing here.”
Duffy has featured in many semi-finals, finals, and even has medals to show for his exploits, but Boldrini is a relative newcomer to the semi-final stage and will feature in just his third.
Talking about his qualification the Italian said: “ It was pretty crazy because I had quite a good round. I didn't expect this result, for me it's crazy, so I'll enjoy it. I’m happy.”
In just his third semi-final appearance, Boldrini isn’t putting too much pressure on himself in the next phase of competition: “I think I just have to go at it and not think about the result. I hope I get more boulders like number three in quali, some campus moves and jumps, I’m a dynamic guy.”
Other climbers making it through are former finalists such as France’s Sam Avezou and Austria’s Jan-Luca Posch, with China’s Yufei Pan hoping he can make the same sort of impact that saw him get a gold in Bern last year.
The two climbers sharing the final spots for progression are Israel’s Adi Bark and Canada’s Matthew Rodriguez in join 23 rd position.
Men's Boulder: https://wclmb.hopp.to/slc26mbr
The women will start their competition with qualification later today. The men will have their semi-final and final tomorrow with the women closing the competition, and Boulder series, with their semi-final and final on Sunday.
News and updates about the World Climbing Series Salt Lake City 2026 will be available on the World Climbing website , and on the Federation’s digital channels: Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , Threads , TikTok , X , YouTube , and exclusively for the Chinese audience, Bilibili, Douyin, Weibo , and Xiaohongshu.

articles.title_orig: After Six Flags Roller Coaster Death, Critics Call for Federal Oversight
articles.title_zh: After Six Flags Roller Coaster Death, Critics Call for Federal Oversight
articles.content_orig:
ATLANTA -- Hassan Kariem 's family is remembering him as a dedicated father, husband, and brother.
"He loved everything about Atlanta. He loved kids. He loved technology," said Joshua Nelson, Kariem's brother-in-law.
SEE ALSO | Six Flags Over Georgia to reopen as planned Friday as Goliath coaster remains closed after fatal fall
Kariem's wife and daughter, along with his niece, all went to Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday to celebrate a birthday. Kariem's daughter was turning 13 years old.
"His last words were to my daughter, and they were, 'This is my favorite ride. I'm so excited to be here,'" Nelson said.
Investigators say Kariem was ejected from the Goliath coaster and fell to his death on Monday. Nelson says his daughter sat right next to Kariem.
READ MORE | Eyewitnesses describe rider's harrowing fall in fatal Six Flags roller coaster incident
"How she described it was, he went up. I guess as the ride was going, he would go up, he went down, went up, down, and the third or fourth time it happened, the latch came undone, and that's when he fell out," Nelson said. "When it first happened, she called me when they got her off the ride, crying. She was like, I don't know where he went."
The Georgia Office of Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire says the Goliath was last inspected in March and showed no warning signs . But Nelson says the family is patiently holding out for answers.
"We're banding together and once the investigation is done, give him the proper sendoff," he said.

articles.title_orig: Reflections | How China’s macabre practice of human sacrifice in burials came to an end
articles.title_zh: Reflections | How China’s macabre practice of human sacrifice in burials came to an end
articles.content_orig:
In China, elites were buried with human companions as far back as the Neolithic period. Over time, symbolic figures replaced real people
Archaeologists have long found a disturbing pattern in the graves of ancient rulers: the dead were sometimes accompanied by other dead. Around royal tombs, the remains of people – who appear to have been killed specifically to follow their masters into the afterlife – lie alongside precious objects and weapons.
A new study from Egypt has brought this practice back into the news. At the ancient royal cemetery of Abydos, archaeologists re-examined the skulls of people buried around the tombs of early rulers. They found signs of serious injuries on many of the skulls, including fractures consistent with powerful blows inflicted around the time of death.
The pattern suggests that at least some of these people did not simply die naturally and happen to be buried near their rulers. They may have been deliberately killed to accompany them into the next world.
Human sacrifice was part of funerary rites of the powerful across the ancient world, from Egypt and Mesopotamia to Europe and the Americas. The practice was also a feature of elite society in ancient China, where it rested on the belief that the dead continued to exist in another world and would need servants, attendants and companions.
